doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Allen Eager record date, Teddy Reig and Duke Jordan's Jordu
summary: At his first big record date Gibbs did not know the Jordu release changes, Duke Jordan wouldn't help, and Teddy Reig stormed into the booth.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Was there a recording, one of your early recordings that you did that there was some issue you wrote about with, because it was a —

Yeah. [inaudible] I think it was my first big record date with Allen Eager. Allen Eager — you know who Teddy “Fats” Reig was? Teddy Reig was the first guy to ever record Bird and Diz, for Savoy Records. He ran that company. And Teddy weighed about 400 pounds. And Allen Eager was the hot white tenor player. He was like the first guy that played like Prez, not that well known. But he had be — he played bebop but like Prez. And he played with Bird and Diz and Miles and all those people. Well Allen loved me and Allen had a great, wild sense of humor, so he loved my dumb sense of humor. So he hired me to do this record date. Now I was leaving the next day to join the Tommy Dorsey Band. So I had my vibes at home all packed up and I had a straight vibes set, and I came in and, there’s never any music you know. What do you play? He played a riff — I played two riffs and Allen put his name on the songs, and not until thirty years later, because Allen unfortunately in those days was hooked on dope but later on when he got himself straightened out I met him in Florida and he kind of apologized for that. But anyhow, we were recording and Duke, you know, I mentioned the chord change was different. Everything was “I Got Rhythm” kind of chord changes. Duke Jordan wrote “Jordu,” which was the middle part or the release or whatever they want to call it, it had different kind of chord changes. And I didn’t know them. I didn’t know the song. So © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Allen said, “You want to play ‘Jordu’?” and I said, “play the melody and I’ll learn” you know. It was really fast. He played it and I played it right after him. And so you know we always played short choruses, maybe 16 bars, because records in those days were three minutes. So but I didn’t know the release chord changes. So I walked over to Duke, who was out in the boonies mentally at the time, he was stoned out, and I said to him, I whispered in his ear, I said, “Duke, what’s the changes in the release?” He said, “Hey why don’t you listen?” I said, “I am listening but I can’t get it.” He says, “Well you’ve got to listen.” And he wouldn’t tell me. So I told Allen, “Allen, I don’t know the release.” He said, “Oh just don’t worry about it, just play the melody.” So anyhow I was the new hot young kid on the block so as we’re playing, and we get to the last chorus, I’m not playing anything at all, Teddy Reig stops the thing and he says, “Hey, why isn’t Terry playing?” And he starts walking out into the thing, and he can hardly get through the door he was that big, you know, seriously. And Allen called, “Hey you fat F-, get back in the booth or I’m going home.” Because Allen was with me.” He says, “Terry doesn’t want to play on this song.” That was the end of that. And so — but Duke wouldn’t tell me the chord changes to the middle part that time. And so I made sure I learned those changes and played the heck out of it.
